title: How Do We Know Jeremiah Preached for About 40 Years?
paragraphs:
How Do We Know Jeremiah Preached for About 40 Years?
The Prophet Who Watched a Nation Collapse—and Still Refused to Stop Speaking God's Truth
There are moments in life when obedience seems to produce nothing.
You pray, but nothing changes.
You love people, yet they reject you.
You tell the truth, and somehow you become the enemy.
If you've ever wondered whether faithfulness is worth it when nobody seems to listen, then the life of Jeremiah may become one of the most comforting—and convicting—stories you'll ever read.
He wasn't the prophet of revival.
He was the prophet who watched a nation ignore God until judgment became unavoidable.

He spent roughly four decades delivering God's message, often with tears running down his face, only to see very little visible success. Yet heaven never measured Jeremiah by popularity. Heaven measured him by faithfulness.
And perhaps that's exactly what many of us need to hear today.
Because our world celebrates results.
God celebrates obedience.
The remarkable thing is that we don't merely estimate Jeremiah's ministry from tradition. Scripture itself provides the timeline.
Jeremiah tells us exactly when God first called him:
"The word of the LORD came to me in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign." (Jeremiah 1:2, ESV)
The Hebrew text begins:
"דְּבַר־יְהוָה" (Devar-YHWH)
Literally,
"The Word of Yahweh."
This wasn't Jeremiah's opinion.
It wasn't political commentary.
It wasn't motivational speaking.
It was God's own revelation entrusted to an ordinary man.
King Josiah began reigning around 640 BC. His thirteenth year places Jeremiah's calling around 627 or 626 BC.
Jeremiah continued ministering through the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah until Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC.
That alone accounts for about forty years of prophetic ministry.
The book itself confirms this span.
Jeremiah 25:3 says:
"For twenty-three years... the word of the LORD has come to me and I have spoken persistently to you, but you have not listened."
Those words were spoken during the fourth year of Jehoiakim's reign. Twenty-three years had already passed since Jeremiah's calling.
Yet the story didn't end there.

Jeremiah continued preaching through another king, witnessed the destruction of Jerusalem, survived imprisonment, persecution, public humiliation, and eventually continued ministering even after the city's collapse.
When these additional years are added together, Scripture presents a ministry lasting approximately forty years.
Not because Jeremiah kept records for historians.
Because God wanted future generations to know what faithful endurance looks like.
One of the most heartbreaking verses comes from Jeremiah 7:27:
"So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you."
Imagine receiving that assignment from God.
"Preach."
"They won't listen."
"Keep preaching anyway."
Most of us secretly hope obedience guarantees visible success.
Jeremiah teaches something different.
Faithfulness sometimes means planting seeds you'll never see grow.
The Hebrew word often translated "listen" is שָׁמַע (shāmaʿ).
It means far more than simply hearing sounds.
It means to hear with the intention of obeying.
Judah heard Jeremiah's voice.
They simply refused to obey God's voice.
How tragically similar that feels today.
Churches can be full.
Bibles can stay open.
Christian content can fill our feeds.
Yet hearing is not the same as surrender.
Jesus would later echo this same truth centuries afterward.
In Greek, He repeatedly declared:
"Ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω."
(Ho echōn ōta akouein akouetō.)
"He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
(Matthew 11:15)
Not everyone who hears truly listens.
Jeremiah understood this long before the Gospel accounts were written.
His own heart became a mirror of God's grief.
He is often called "the Weeping Prophet," not because he lacked courage, but because he loved people enough to cry over the judgment they refused to escape.
In Jeremiah 9:1 he laments:
"Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears..."
The Hebrew expression paints a vivid image of tears flowing without end.
God's warnings were never motivated by cruelty.
They flowed from divine compassion.
Judgment was God's strange work.
Mercy was always His desire.
That reaches its fullest expression in Jesus Christ.
Jeremiah faithfully proclaimed coming judgment.
Jesus willingly bore that judgment Himself.
Centuries before the cross, Jeremiah announced humanity's need.
At Calvary, Christ became God's answer.
Isaiah declared,
"He was pierced for our transgressions..." (Isaiah 53:5)
Paul later explained,
"For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God." (2 Corinthians 5:21)
The Gospel is not that humanity became better.
The Gospel is that Jesus stepped into our place.
Our rebellion met His mercy.
Our guilt met His grace.
Our scandal met His cross.
And because of His resurrection, our ending no longer has to be defined by our beginning.
That is why our heartbeat remains the same:
Perhaps you've spent years praying for someone who still hasn't come to Christ.
Perhaps you've tried to live faithfully while your workplace mocks your convictions.
Perhaps you've wondered whether your quiet obedience even matters.
Jeremiah's life answers with a resounding yes.
Success in God's kingdom is never measured first by applause.
It is measured by faithfulness.
For nearly forty years Jeremiah proclaimed the Word of Yahweh whether people celebrated him or rejected him.
He trusted that God was responsible for the results.
His responsibility was simply to remain faithful.
The same calling rests upon every believer today.
Not all are prophets.
But every Christian is called to bear witness to Christ with truth, humility, compassion, and perseverance.
Your faithfulness may become the sermon someone remembers years from now.
Your quiet obedience may become the seed God uses long after you're gone.
Never underestimate what God does through those who simply refuse to quit.
Someone in your circle may be silently wondering whether following Christ is worth the cost, and this may be the encouragement they need today.
God often uses ordinary acts of sharing to begin extraordinary conversations about eternity.
If this message strengthened your faith, save it so you can return to it whenever discouragement whispers that obedience is pointless.
Before you leave, we'd love to hear from you.
Have you ever gone through a season where you stayed faithful even though you couldn't see the results?
Your story may encourage another believer who feels like giving up today.
One simple sentence may become someone else's reminder to keep following Christ.
Because sometimes the greatest victories are the ones only heaven sees.
